notes.text: For more than 8, brown the chicken in three batches instead of two, so the pan never gets crowded.

move.title: Brown it, then glaze it
move.body: Building a sauce means adding flavors one layer at a time. Today you'll brown bite-size chicken, then pour in a honey, soy, and garlic sauce and let it bubble down until it's thick and sticky and clings to every piece. Rice cooks on the next burner.

why.title: A light coat of cornstarch
why.body: Tossing the chicken in cornstarch gives each piece a thin coat. In the hot pan it turns golden and a little crisp. Later, it grabs the sauce and helps thicken it, so the glaze sticks instead of sliding off.

why.title: Give it room
why.body: Chicken gives off juice as it cooks. With space around each piece, the juice boils away fast and the chicken browns. Crowd the pan and the juice pools, and the chicken steams pale instead. That's why it cooks in two batches.

why.title: Bubbling it down
why.body: As the sauce bubbles, water escapes as steam. What's left is thicker and stronger: honey and soy turn into a shiny glaze. The bubbles tell you: small and fast at first, then bigger, slower, and stickier as it thickens.

why.title: Honey burns fast
why.body: Honey is sugar, and sugar goes from golden to burnt in moments. Keep the heat at medium once the sauce is in, and keep stirring. If it smells smoky, pull the pan off the heat right away.

wrong.sign: The chicken is pale and sitting in juice
wrong.fix: The pan was crowded or not hot enough. Turn the heat up and let the juice boil away before stirring. Cook the next batch with fewer pieces.

wrong.sign: The sauce is thin and runny
wrong.fix: Keep it bubbling a minute or two more, stirring. It thickens more as it cools, too.

wrong.sign: The sauce smells smoky or looks dark brown
wrong.fix: Take the pan off the heat and stir in 2 tablespoons of water. Next time, use lower heat once the honey goes in.
Serve it with more rice, and use a little less soy sauce next time.

quiz.q: Why does the chicken brown in two batches?
choices: So it browns instead of steaming
quiz.explain: Crowded chicken sits in its own juice and steams. With room, the juice boils off and it browns.

quiz.q: How can you tell the sauce has thickened?
choices: The bubbles get big, slow, and sticky
quiz.explain: As water boils away, the bubbles slow down and the sauce turns glossy and coats the chicken.

steps.text: Put the rice in the saucepan and cover it with cold water. Swish it with your hand, then carefully pour off the cloudy water, holding the rice back with your hand. Do this 3 times.
steps.tip: Rinsing washes off loose starch, so the rice cooks up fluffy instead of gluey.

steps.text: Add {qty:water} of water to the rice. Bring it to a boil over high heat with the lid off. Then turn the heat to low, put the lid on, and cook without lifting the lid.
steps.tip: When the timer rings, turn off the burner and leave the lid on. The rice keeps steaming while you finish the chicken.

steps.text: Peel and mince the garlic. Scrape the skin off the ginger with the edge of a spoon, then grate it on the small holes of the grater. In the small bowl, stir together the honey, soy sauce, rice vinegar, a splash of water, the garlic, and the ginger.
steps.tip: Grate the ginger slowly. The piece gets small fast, so stop before your fingers get near the holes.

steps.text: Slice the green onions into thin rings.
Cut the chicken into 1-inch pieces and put them in the large bowl. Sprinkle on the cornstarch, {qty:salt} salt, and the pepper, and toss with the spoon until every piece is coated.
Wash your hands, the knife, and the cutting board with hot, soapy water.
steps.tip: Raw chicken can carry germs. Wash before you touch anything else.

steps.text: Heat half the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
Tip half the chicken into the pan and spread it into one layer with the spatula.
steps.tip: Tip it in close to the pan, away from you, so the oil doesn't splash.

steps.text: Leave the chicken alone until it's brown underneath, then stir and cook until golden all over. Move it to the plate.
steps.look: Golden-brown on most sides, with no pink on the outside.

steps.text: Add the rest of the oil. Tip in the rest of the chicken and spread it out.
Wash your hands with soap, and wash the bowl the chicken was in.
Brown the second batch the same way.

Put all the chicken back in the pan and turn the heat down to medium. Stir the sauce (the garlic sinks) and pour it in. Let it bubble, stirring often, until it's thick and sticky and coats the chicken.
steps.look: Big, slow, sticky bubbles, and a shiny glaze on every piece.
steps.tip: Bubbling honey is hotter than boiling water. Keep your hands back and stir with the long spatula.

steps.text: Turn off the heat. Slide the thermometer into the thickest piece of chicken. It needs to read at least 165°F. If it doesn't, cook 2 more minutes on low, stirring, and check again.
Fluff the rice with the fork. Spoon the chicken and its glaze over the rice, and sprinkle with green onions and the sesame seeds if you're using them.

notes.text: For more than 8, brown the salmon in three batches instead of two, so the pan never gets crowded.

cut-chicken.text: Pat the salmon dry with paper towels. Cut it into 1-inch pieces and put them in the large bowl. Sprinkle on the cornstarch, {qty:salt} salt, and the pepper, and toss gently with the spoon until every piece is coated.

wash-1.text: Wash your hands, the knife, and the cutting board with hot, soapy water.
wash-1.tip: Raw fish can carry germs. Wash before you touch anything else.

batch-1.text: Gently tip half the salmon into the pan and spread it into one layer with the spatula.
batch-1.tip: Tip it in close to the pan, away from you, so the oil doesn't splash.

brown-1.text: Leave the salmon alone until it's golden underneath, about 2 minutes. Turn the pieces gently and brown another side. Move them to the plate.
brown-1.look: Golden on two sides, and no longer see-through on the outside.

batch-2.text: Add the rest of the oil. Gently tip in the rest of the salmon and spread it out.

wash-3.text: Wash your hands with soap, and wash the bowl the salmon was in.

brown-2.text: Brown the second batch the same way.

glaze.text: Turn the heat down to medium. Stir the sauce (the garlic sinks) and pour it into the empty pan. Let it bubble, stirring often, until it's thick and sticky.
glaze.tip: Bubbling honey is hotter than boiling water. Keep your hands back and stir with the long spatula.

check-chicken.text: Turn off the heat. Slide the thermometer into the thickest piece of salmon. It needs to read at least 145°F. If it doesn't, cook 1 more minute on low and check again.

serve.text: Fluff the rice with the fork. Spoon the salmon and its glaze over the rice, and sprinkle with green onions and the sesame seeds if you're using them.

add.text: Put all the salmon back in the pan and turn the pieces gently in the glaze until every one is shiny.

Serve it with more rice, and use a little less soy sauce next time.

wrong.sign: The salmon is breaking into flakes
wrong.fix: It's still good to eat. Turn it more gently, and stir the glaze around it instead of stirring the salmon.

coat.title: A light coat of cornstarch
coat.body: Tossing the salmon in cornstarch gives each piece a thin coat. In the hot pan it turns golden and a little crisp. Later, it grabs the sauce, so the glaze sticks instead of sliding off.

crowd.title: Give it room
crowd.body: Salmon gives off juice as it cooks. With space around each piece, the juice boils away fast and the salmon browns. Crowd the pan and the juice pools, and the salmon steams pale instead. That's why it cooks in two batches.

add.title: Gentle with fish
add.body: Salmon is soft, and it flakes apart as it cooks. It also cooks much faster than chicken. Turn the pieces gently with a thin spatula, and take them out as soon as they're golden. The sauce bubbles down on its own, and the salmon goes back in at the end.

notes.text: For more than 8, brown the tofu in three batches instead of two, so the pan never gets crowded.

cut-chicken.text: Unwrap the tofu and cut it into 1-inch cubes. Put them in the large bowl, sprinkle on the cornstarch, {qty:salt} salt, and the pepper, and toss gently with the spoon until every piece is coated.

batch-1.text: Tip half the tofu into the pan and spread it into one layer with the spatula.
batch-1.tip: Tip it in close to the pan, away from you, so the oil doesn't splash.

brown-1.text: Leave the tofu alone until it's golden underneath, then turn the pieces and brown the other sides. Move it to the plate.
brown-1.look: Golden and crisp on most sides.

batch-2.text: Add the rest of the oil. Tip in the rest of the tofu and spread it out.

brown-2.text: Brown the second batch the same way.

glaze.text: Put all the tofu back in the pan and turn the heat down to medium. Stir the sauce (the garlic sinks) and pour it in. Let it bubble, stirring gently, until it's thick and sticky and coats the tofu.
glaze.look: Big, slow, sticky bubbles, and a shiny glaze on every piece.
glaze.tip: Bubbling honey is hotter than boiling water. Keep your hands back and stir with the long spatula.

serve.text: Turn off the heat. Fluff the rice with the fork. Spoon the tofu and its glaze over the rice, and sprinkle with green onions and the sesame seeds if you're using them.

add.text: Drain the tofu. Wrap each block in the kitchen towel, lay them on a plate, and set a heavy pan on top to press out the water.
add.tip: Start the rice while the tofu presses.

move.title: Brown it, then glaze it
move.body: Building a sauce means adding flavors one layer at a time. Today you'll press and brown cubes of tofu, then pour in a honey, soy, and garlic sauce and let it bubble down until it's thick and sticky and clings to every piece. Rice cooks on the next burner.

wrong.sign: The tofu is pale and soft
wrong.fix: It needed more pressing, or the pan was crowded. Turn the heat up and give each piece room. Press the next block longer.

wrong.sign: The sauce is thin and runny
wrong.fix: Keep it bubbling a minute or two more, stirring. It thickens more as it cools, too.

wrong.sign: The sauce smells smoky or looks dark brown
wrong.fix: Take the pan off the heat and stir in 2 tablespoons of water. Next time, use lower heat once the honey goes in.
Serve it with more rice, and use a little less soy sauce next time.
Use extra-firm tofu, and turn the pieces gently with the spatula instead of stirring hard.

quiz.q: Why do you press the tofu first?
choices: To squeeze out water so it browns
quiz.explain: Wet tofu steams. Pressed tofu browns and crisps in the hot pan.

quiz.q: How can you tell the sauce has thickened?
choices: The bubbles get big, slow, and sticky
quiz.explain: As water boils away, the bubbles slow down and the sauce turns glossy and coats the chicken.

coat.title: A light coat of cornstarch
coat.body: Tossing the tofu in cornstarch gives each piece a thin coat. In the hot pan it turns golden and crisp. Later, it grabs the sauce and helps thicken it, so the glaze sticks instead of sliding off.

crowd.title: Give it room
crowd.body: Tofu still has some water in it. With space around each piece, the water boils away fast and the tofu browns. Crowd the pan and the steam has nowhere to go, so the tofu stays pale and soft. That's why it cooks in two batches.

add.title: Why press the tofu
add.body: Tofu is packed in water, and wet tofu steams in the pan instead of browning. Pressing it under a weight squeezes the water out, so the outside can turn golden and crisp.
